title: Tables on a marketing site
excerpt: A comparison table works when the rows are real differences a buyer can use. A grid of checkmarks that are all checked is an advertisement, and readers can tell.
alt: Crates of used books at an outdoor stall, titles facing out, a set of real options for an article about comparison tables with actual differences.
caption: Titles facing out, so you can tell the books apart. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a marketing site use a table?
faqs.answer: Use a table when a buyer is comparing a few options along the same questions, such as what is included, what is not, and who each option is for. If the information is a story, write a story. If every cell would say yes, you do not have a comparison, and a short list of what is included will be more honest.

faqs.question: How do you keep a pricing table honest?
faqs.answer: Make the rows the decisions that actually change between plans. Limits, support, who the plan is for, and what is excluded. Identical checkmarks across every column teach the reader to ignore the grid. Put the difference in words, not only in a mark, so the cell still means something when it is read aloud or copied.

faqs.question: What makes a table readable on a phone?
faqs.answer: Keep the number of columns small enough to compare, and give each column a real header. Let the row header stay visible as they move across, or stack each plan as its own labeled block that repeats the questions. A table that requires a precise sideways hunt, with no headers, is a spreadsheet you published by accident.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Data table design marketing pages get wrong when they use a table as a poster. A comparison works when the rows are real differences: what this plan includes, what the other does not, who each one is for. A grid of checkmarks that are all checked is an advertisement. Readers can tell, and they stop reading the grid.

Use a table when the buyer is trying to choose. Use sentences when you are trying to explain. Mixing those jobs in one green wall of ticks helps nobody make the choice.

## Rows that are allowed to differ

Start from the questions a buyer actually asks. Can I do the core job. What is the limit. Who is it for. What happens when I need a human. What is not included. Each of those can be a row. If two columns would have the same answer, the row is not a comparison. It can be a sentence above the table: "Every plan includes the export." Then the table can spend its rows on the split.

Write the cell as words when the difference is not yes or no. "Email support in two business days" versus "A shared channel with a named contact" is a difference. A check in both columns is a blur. Checks are fine for a true binary, and they should be the word "included" or "not included" as well, so the meaning does not depend on a glyph. [The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the reference for information that has to be understandable without a single sense. A checkmark that is only a shape, with no text, fails that, and it fails the person who copies the cell into a note.

Three or four columns are a choice. Seven columns are a spreadsheet. If you have seven products, you may be looking at a filter or a guided question, not a table. Ask which comparison a single buyer makes. Usually it is two or three neighbors, not the entire catalog. Show those. Link to the rest.

[Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people often leave a page within 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear in about 10, and that they read only about a quarter of the text. A table has to be scannable inside that attention. The first column, the row labels, should be the questions. The column headers should be the options. If they have to study the legend before any cell makes sense, the table arrived too late in its own explanation.

## Pricing tables, specifically

A pricing table is a promise about the shape of the price. Show what changes the number. Seats, usage, a setup, a line you will not cross. If the price is custom, a table can still show what a conversation will cover, and what it will not. Hiding the shape because the number varies forces every buyer into a call to learn they are in the wrong range.

Put the recommended option in words, not only in a colored column. "Fits teams that already have a weekly export" is a reason. A badge that says Popular is a nudge with no content. You can use both. The reason has to be able to stand if the color is stripped. Highlighting a column is fine when the highlight is not the only way to know which one you mean.

Do not check every feature in the expensive column and half of them in the cheap one if the cheap plan is a trap. Technical buyers notice a table that punishes the smaller plan with missing basics, such as security or export, while the prose above says you are friendly to small teams. Align the prose and the grid. If the small plan is real, let it look real. If it is a decoy, you do not need it on the page.

Name the unit. Per month, billed annually, in dollars, excluding tax. A table that says "29" without a unit is a riddle. The unit can live in the header so you do not repeat it in every cell. Repeat it if any cell is a different unit. Mixed units in an unlabeled grid are how people feel misled after they talk to sales.

## Headers, scope, and the words

The top header names the option. The first cell of each row names the question. Those are headers, and they should be marked as headers so a screen reader can announce "Support, Team plan, shared channel" instead of a loose string of words. This is ordinary table structure, and it is also what makes the visual design clearer. A bold first column is not a decoration. It is the list of questions.

Keep the vocabulary identical to the product. If the app says workspace, the row says workspace. A marketing table that invents "hub" for the brochure will be quoted back to you on the call, and the demo will not contain a hub. The noun list is doing sales work here. Let it.

Caption the table with the decision it supports. "What changes between the three plans." A caption is not a second headline full of adjectives. It tells a skimmer whether to engage. Under the table, one sentence can name the exception: "Agencies with more than one brand need a conversation, because these plans assume one." That sentence prevents the table from lying by omission.

Do not merge cells to be clever. Merged headers are hard to read and harder to hear. If two plans share a detail, write it above the table and remove the row. Simpler grids get used. Complex grids get screenshotted and misunderstood in a slide.

## Phones, and the temptation to scroll sideways

A marketing table will be opened on a phone, often forwarded there. Wide grids fail. You have a few honest options. Fewer columns. A stacked layout where each plan is a headed block and the questions repeat. A control that switches the visible plan while the questions stay put. What you should not do is a tiny table that requires a precise horizontal flick, with the row labels scrolling away.

Test the stack. Read one plan from top to bottom. The questions should still be next to the answers. A stack that shows values without repeating the questions is a list of mysteries. Repeat the label. Redundancy is the point on a small screen.

Touch targets and type size follow the rest of the site. A table is not an excuse for 11-pixel type. If the content does not fit at a readable size, you have too many rows or too many words in a cell. Edit the cell. Do not shrink the type until it fits. The buyer is comparing, not decoding.

Sticky headers can help on a long table, if they do not cover the row you are reading and if they remain headers. Test them with a keyboard and with a phone. A sticky bar that traps focus or hides the next row is a craft bug, even if the desktop demo looked slick. Motion, if the switch between plans animates, should be short and should respect reduced motion. The numbers matter more than the glide.

## When a table is the wrong object

Use a list when there is one offer and you are enumerating what is in it. A one-column table of checks is a list that learned bad manners. Write the list. People know how to read it.

Use prose when the difference needs a condition. "Included if your workspace was created after April, otherwise we migrate it with you." A cell cannot hold that without becoming a paragraph, and a paragraph in every cell means you wanted an article. Give the condition its own short section, and let the table stay binary where it is truly binary.

Use nothing when you do not know the difference yet. An empty comparison, filled with checks so the page does not look sparse, trains buyers to distrust the next true table you publish. Leave the space blank and write the sentence you can stand behind. Sparsity is more credible than decoration.

Competitors' names in a table are a legal and a factual risk, and they go stale. If you compare, compare on facts you can source and date the table. If you cannot, compare your own plans, or compare approaches in the abstract without a smear. A stale cell will be the one a buyer quotes. Dated, specific, and narrow beats broad and brave.

## How to review the grid

Read each column as a person. Could they choose it and know what they will not get. If every column sounds like a winner, you hid the tradeoff. Put the tradeoff back. Buyers who cannot see a tradeoff assume you are hiding it, which is worse than stating a limit.

Read each row across. Does the wording stay parallel. "2 hours" and "priority" are not parallel, and the eye cannot compare them. Pick a unit for the row. Time, or a named channel, or a limit. Parallel cells are the whole point of the alignment.

Ask someone who was not in the pricing meeting to pick a column for a scenario you describe. If they pick wrong, the row labels failed, or the difference is imaginary. Fix the labels before you restyle the header. A beautiful header on a confusing row is still a miss. The buyer's question lives in the row.

On a Hanabi page, a table is a component with real headers, in the same type ramp as the site, built so it does not shift the layout when it loads. Cumulative layout shift is a polite way to say the page jumped. A table that pops in and shoves the call to action down will be blamed on the offer, not on the grid. Reserve the space. Then let the words do the work.

## The limit of comparison

A fair table will not close a deal that the product cannot serve. It will prevent the wrong deal, which is a success the analytics will undercount. Track the conversations that arrive already sorted, not only the clicks on the highlighted column. If everyone still asks the same question, that question is a missing row or a missing sentence above the grid.

Do not let the table become the only way to talk. Some buyers need a person. The action beside the table should say what the conversation is for, especially if a column says "contact us" with no hint of the agenda. A button under a grid is still a promise. Write it as carefully as the cells.

People who never reach the table, or who pass it and are still lost, end up in the footer. [Footers that help](/blog/footers-that-help) is about repeating the action, the legal facts, and a few real destinations for that person. Read it when the comparison is honest and the bottom of the page is still a junk drawer.

If you want a second look at whether a grid is a comparison or a poster, book [an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the table and the question you hope it answers. If the rows do not answer it, the call should end with a shorter table, or with none.
